query: In September, how did refined oil product flows from the Gulf region compare with preconflict levels?

results.text: Several producers outside the Gulf have ramped up output, collectively adding nearly 2.2 mb/d, on average, since the conflict began, while trading patterns have adjusted to connect importers usually dependent on the Gulf with alternative suppliers. In 2026Q2, during the deepest supply shortfalls in the Middle East, shifts in oil trade in the United States and China illustrated these trends. U.S. exports of crude oil and oil products increased by about 1.7 mb/d relative to February, enabled by inventory releases and a pickup in production, while China’s imports declined by more than 5 mb/d as refinery runs fell and oil stocks were drawn (figure 1.C). The global oil production surplus last year, which exceeded 2 mb/d in 2025Q4, also reduced the extent of the adjustments to global demand (figure 1.D).

In the Gulf, required repairs to damaged facilities are likely to delay a full return of refinery throughput to pre-conflict levels until 2027Q2. Even as crude flows return, the normalization of the oil market is anticipated to be slow and potentially halting in the absence of a comprehensive resolution to the conflict. Regional oil-transport bottlenecks are expected to linger as limited tanker availability, shipowners’ reluctance to transit high-risk routes, and continued reliance FIGURE 8 Oil market: Demand and supply Global oil consumption is projected to fall by 2.6 mb/d in 2026, owing to the effects of high prices and supply shortages. The decline is clustered in EMDEs, with sizeable falls occurring in China, Russia and several Gulf economies.

The prospective surplus is contingent on the availability of viable trade routes, limited long- term damage to production facilities in the Middle East, and continued supply growth outside the Middle East. With supply projected to exceed consumption by about 2 mb/d on average over the final three quarters of 2027, inventories are expected to rise by about 550 mb by year-end, reversing roughly 80 percent of the 2026 drawdown. That said, it is quite likely that aggregate desired inventories will exceed their levels prior to the Middle East conflict, given the scale of disruptions and inventory reliance this year. Global refinery throughput is projected to fall by 2.3 mb/d in 2026, recover in 2027, and rise further in 2028. The rebound is expected to come from three sources. In the Gulf, completion of repairs to damaged facilities is expected to restore throughput to pre-conflict levels.

query: By how much had the World Bank Group's metals and minerals index risen in 2026 relative to the first nine months of 2025?

results.text: Over the five years through 2030, the World Bank Group is targeting a fivefold increase in financing of the metals and minerals sector, to $19 billion, to support mineral-rich EMDEs in converting their natural endowments into lasting prosperity. T o foster dynamic private sectors and help create jobs more broadly, the World Bank Group has accelerated and simplified its ability to catalyze private capital flows alongside its financing and knowledge services. Through enhanced private capital mobilization, the institution will seek to deepen investment in the next generation of youth in client countries—in particular, by improving the conditions for job creation.

Metal prices are forecast to inch down in 2027, but a high-price regime is expected to remain entrenched, with the metals and minerals price index projected to exceed its 2021 peak by 16 percent. Demand for base metals is anticipated to hold firm, underpinned by robust investment in electrification infrastructure, renewable energy, and data centers, which are base-metal-intensive. However, subdued conventional construction in many economies and weakness in China’s steel sector are likely to weigh on iron ore prices. The precious metals price index fell by 7 percent in 2026Q3 after reaching all-time highs earlier in the year. Still, the index is on track to increase by 40 percent in 2026, before drifting lower by 8 percent in 2027 as investor demand moderates.

query: How many people experienced severe food insecurity worldwide in 2025?

results.text: The number of people experiencing severe food insecurity worldwide fell to about 779 million in 2025 from 803 million in 2024 and 837 million in 2021 (figure 15.B). The 21 percent decline in global food commodity prices between 2022 and 2025 likely contributed to these gains. Even so, severe food insecurity affected 9.5 percent of the global population in 2025, well above the 8.1 percent average in the five years before COVID-19. With food prices forecast to rise by a cumulative 18 percent in 2026–27 amid overlapping weather, logistics, and conflict shocks, this tailwind for the fight against hunger appears set to become a headwind. These challenges are compounded by surging energy prices, which strain household budgets and further erode food affordability.

People experiencing severe food insecurity worldwide numbered 779 million in 2025, down from 803 million in 2024 and 837 million in 2021. Even so, efforts to reduce food insecurity have regressed since the 2010s: severe food insecurity affected 9.5 percent of the global population in 2025, compared with an average of 8.1 percent in 2015–19 (figure 6.B). Moreover, the baseline outlook brings an end to the tailwind from falling global food commodity prices between 2023 and 2025, which had put downward pressure on consumer food costs. In this context, EMDE food price inflation picked up to a median of 3.9 percent (y/y) in 2026Q3, from 3.5 percent the previous quarter, and may firm further as sizable increases in grain and oilseed prices feed through.

The recent price increase reflects excessive rainfall in Brazil (the world’s largest coffee producer), FIGURE 15 Food price inflation and food insecurity Domestic food inflation in EMDEs increased in 2026Q3, particularly in the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan, South Asia, and Sub-Saharan Africa regions, and it could rise further, particularly given the forecast increases in the prices of grains and edible oils. The number of people experiencing severe food insecurity globally declined slightly in 2025. However, food insecurity remains more prevalent than in the late 2010s, and renewed food price increases anticipated in 2026–27 could reverse recent progress. Sources: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAOSTAT database); Haver Analytics; World Bank.

query: In the energy section, what drove Gulf voyage rates to record highs?

results.text: Crude oil prices rose sharply in 2026Q3 as hopes for a near-term end to hostilities faded and renewed attacks heightened concerns about Gulf supplies. The increase coincided with a partial recovery in China’s imports and renewed drawdowns in global inventories. Amid material damage to refineries in the Gulf region, product markets also tightened, particularly for diesel, with the European diesel premium rising to nearly $90/bbl in September. Sources: Bloomberg; General Administration of Customs of the People’s Republic of China; International Energy Agency (IEA); Reuters; World Bank. Note: bbl = barrel; mb = million barrels; mb/d = million barrels per day. A. Two-day average of daily spot (dated Brent) and front-month Brent futures prices. Last observation is October 14, 2026. B. Daily data, averaged semi-monthly.

Natural gas Recent developments Natural gas markets in most regions tightened sharply in 2026Q3 as Middle East tensions re-escalated and the June U.S.–Iran MoU failed to produce a follow-on agreement. Concerns about prolonged Gulf supply disruptions, stronger Asian power-sector demand, and low European inventories drove up European natural gas and Asian LNG prices to more than double their pre-conflict levels by September, with prices continuing to increase in October (figure 10.A). Although LNG shipments via the Strait of Hormuz have started to increase in recent weeks, they remained at about 25 percent of pre-conflict levels in September. Before the recent resurgence, prices had plunged in June after the MoU was signed and backed up LNG cargoes exited the Gulf. In contrast, monthly U.S. natural gas prices were generally below February levels in 2026Q3,

Shortages of some refined fuels have become acute: average U.S. diesel prices reached record levels in October. Amid depleted liquefied natural gas (LNG) shipments, European natural gas prices are slated to jump by almost 60 percent this year. Average energy prices are forecast to decrease by about 12 percent in 2027, with Brent oil retreating to $79 per barrel. This forecast assumes a continued gradual increase in crude oil exports from the Middle East, aided by pipeline flows and workarounds for shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. Yet damaged refineries and gas-export facilities are expected to delay the recovery of diesel and LNG supplies. Near-term risks are tilted toward higher prices, as conflict-driven energy market disruptions could deepen.

query: Why is the reported 7.8 billion barrels of observed oil inventories not all immediately usable?

results.text: ENERGY COMMODITY MARKETS OUTLOOK | OCTOBER 2026 16 Supply losses have persistently exceeded the reduction in global oil demand since the onset of the Middle East conflict, with the deficit widening sharply in 2026Q2 to 2.9 mb/d but narrowing in the following quarter (figure 8.F). Accordingly, oil inventories have become the fulcrum on which oil markets have balanced. Although global observed oil inventories still total about 7.8 billion barrels, much is in transit or tied up operationally—for instance, to keep pipelines pressurized—and therefore is not readily usable. In this context, OECD member governments’ inventories at end-September were the lowest in more than three decades, with the U.S. strategic reserves the lowest since 1982. Global oil markets have thus become increasingly vulnerable to further supply disruptions.

query: What change in global natural gas production is projected for 2026?

results.text: ENERGYCOMMODITY MARKETS OUTLOOK | OCTOBER 2026 21 Global natural gas production is projected to decline by 0.8 percent (35 bcm) in 2026. A drop of more than 11 percent (90 bcm) in the Middle East—driven by damage to gas-processing and LNG facilities—is expected to be partly offset by increases of 3.2 percent (42 bcm) in North America and 2.1 percent (18 bcm) in Eurasia. Global production is forecast to increase by about 2.5 percent (110 bcm) in 2027, led by nearly a 5.5 percent (39 bcm) recovery in the Middle East, with the region’s output expected to remain below its 2025 level because of reduced LNG export capacity in Qatar and delays to its North Field expansion. Production is also expected to rise by 3 percent (41 bcm) in North America, 2 percent (15 bcm) in Asia Pacific, and 1 percent (10 bcm) in Eurasia.

In contrast, the U.S. benchmark is projected to remain unchanged in 2026 (y/y), and to increase by about 6 percent in 2027 and about 5 percent in 2028, mainly driven by growing external demand for LNG. Global natural gas consumption is projected to decline by about 1 percent (50 bcm) in 2026 (figure 10.D). Demand is expected to decrease by about 8 percent (50 bcm) in the Middle East, reflecting disrupted industrial demand. In Europe and Asia Pacific, consumption is set to soften by 2.5 percent (13 bcm) and about 1 percent (9 bcm), respectively, as power-sector use declines. By contrast, Eurasian demand is projected to rise as residential consumption rebounds after mild weather in 2025.

ENERGY COMMODITY MARKETS OUTLOOK | OCTOBER 2026 20 owing to strong domestic production and ample inventories. Global natural gas demand contracted in 2026H1 amid the rise in prices and pronounced LNG supply constraints, in contrast with earlier expectations. The decline was especially sharp in the Middle East, where demand from gas-intensive industries collapsed. Asian consumption fell by 1 percent (5 bcm) (y/y), led by a 2.4 percent (5.1 bcm) drop in China, amid mild weather, gas-to- coal switching in the power sector, and slower industrial production growth. In North America, U.S. consumption declined by about 1.5 percent (7 bcm) despite stable prices, as a mild winter in several regions more than offset stronger gas-fired power demand, owing in part to rising data-center power needs.

query: How many very strong El Niño episodes had occurred since 1950 before the current episode?

results.text: Episodes of El Niño vary considerably in intensity (figure B1.2.A).a Since 1950, there have been 27 El Niño episodes, four of which were very strong (in 1982–83, 1991–92, 1997–98, and 2015–16), with the current episode expected to become the fifth. Over the same period, there were 3 strong, 9 moderate, and 11 weak episodes. El Niño episodes typically emerge around May or June, strengthen through the third quarter of the year, peak near year-end, and dissipate during the first half of the following year. As a result, much of the associated rainfall anomaly occurs during the second half of the year, overlapping with the growing season for several major internationally traded commodities.

According to the U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Admin- istration (NOAA), El Niño events are classified as weak (RONI of 0.5°C to <1.0°C), moderate (1.0°C to <1.5°C), strong (1.5°C to <2.0°C), or very strong (2.0°C or higher), based on the Relative Oceanic Niño Index (RONI). An event is classified according to the highest category threshold met or exceeded for at least three consecutive overlapping three-month periods. b. Remote links between ENSO and distant weather patterns, known as teleconnections, are typically measured by correlations between an ENSO index and local temperature and precipitation, and are generally strongest in the tropics.

La Niña is the cool phase of ENSO, characterized by below-average sea- surface temperatures in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific. According to NOAA, episodes are defined as five consecutive overlapping three-month periods at or above +0.5°C for El Niño and at or below −0.5°C for La Niña. Horizontal lines indicate the +0.5°C and −0.5°C thresholds. Last observation is August 2026. B. Country-level ENSO teleconnections, based on Callahan and Mankin (2023). Teleconnection scores are calculated as the sum of the absolute values of the correlation coefficients between the E-index and monthly country-level temperature and precipitation from 1960 to 2019. High, medium, and low exposure countries refer to the top, middle, and bottom terciles of the teleconnection score distribution. C.

The products include crude oil and U.S. natural gas in the energy group; aluminum, copper, nickel, and zinc in the industrial metals group; maize, soybeans, and wheat in the food group; live cattle and lean hogs in the livestock group; gold and silver in the precious metals group; and coffee and cotton in the soft commodities group.3 The common sample spans May 5, 2006, the earliest date for which data are available, to June 26, 2026. Price volatility is measured using the range-based estimator of Garman and Klass (1980), which combines daily opening, closing, high, and low prices. T o capture relationships across a relatively large number of markets, the analysis estimates an elastic net vector autoregression model (appendix SF .1).

Most commodity analysis appropriately focuses on the supply and demand fundamentals of individual markets. While that approach remains important, it provides only a partial view when volatility associated with one commodity is linked to developments in other commodity markets. This Special Focus examines price volatility connectedness across 15 internationally traded commodities in six groups—energy, food, industrial metals, livestock, precious metals, and soft commodities (such as coffee and cotton)— using daily data from 2006 to 2026. Price volatility connectedness measures how much of the variance in a commodity’s price volatility can be explained by shocks affecting prices in other commodity markets.

SPECIAL FOCUS COMMODITY MARKETS OUTLOOK | OCTOBER 2026 48 Introduction Commodity prices often move in tandem because many markets are exposed to common shifts in global activity, input costs, trade, and financial conditions. For instance, a slowdown in industrial activity can weaken demand for energy and industrial metals at the same time, while disruptions to energy supply can raise transport and fertilizer costs and spill into agricultural markets. Periods of financial or geopolitical stress can broaden these movements across otherwise distinct commodity groups (World Bank 2024). Understanding these linkages is key because commodity price shocks affect inflation, fiscal revenues, trade balances, and food and energy security, particularly in emerging market and developing economies (EMDEs) with large commodity exposures (Balcilar, Usman and Agan 2024; World Bank 2026a).
